Welcome to Accessible HTML5

This is a well-structured, accessible HTML5 document demonstrating modern best practices for semantic markup and inclusive design.

It uses semantic landmarks, a skip link for keyboard navigation, and CSS that adapts to your light or dark mode preference.

Text and link colors meet WCAG AA contrast in both themes, type scales with your browser's font size, and motion respects your system settings.

Features

  • Semantic HTML structure with proper landmarks
  • Keyboard accessible navigation and focus management
  • Dark mode support with custom color schemes
  • Responsive typography using modern CSS
  • Print-friendly styles for better readability
  • WCAG AA contrast compliance in all color modes

Examples

Component Cards

Card components are useful for organizing related content. They include a subtle border and padding for visual separation.

Learn more about accessibility resources

Interactive Elements

Buttons and links are fully accessible with clear focus states. All interactive elements include visible focus indicators and proper ARIA labels.

Keyboard navigation: Use Tab to move forward, Shift+Tab to move backward, and Enter or Space to activate.

lines: +      /* Doubled to outrank the dark theme selectors, which would otherwise reset these borders. */

content.text:
I fixed one bug in `0.html`. The rest of the file (semantics, focus handling, live regions, theming, forms, print styles) was already in good shape, so I didn't change it just for the sake of changing it.

**The bug:** users who have both dark mode and "Increase contrast" turned on lost the high-contrast borders. The high-contrast rule (`0.html:363`) sets `--border` and `--border-control` to `currentColor`, but it used a plain `:root` selector. The dark-theme rules use stronger selectors (`:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and `:root[data-theme="dark"]`), so they won and put back the faint `#333` borders on cards, table rows and the live-region boxes.

**The fix:** I changed the selector to `:root:root`. That makes it as strong as the dark-theme selectors, and because it comes later in the file, it wins. I added a comment explaining why the selector is doubled.

I haven't checked this in a browser. To confirm, emulate `prefers-contrast: more` together with dark mode in your browser's dev tools.

**Smaller things you could change if you want:**
- The canonical link points to `https://www.example.com`, and there's no `og:url`. Both need the real URL before you deploy.
- After a successful form submit, the script moves focus straight back to the email field. A screen reader may then read the field instead of the "Success!" message. You could leave focus where it is, or focus the status message instead.
